scenario: You discover an error in a calculation already sent to a client. The impact seems small, but the client may have used it. You also have another deadline in an hour.

options.A: Correct and resend it immediately, then brief your manager afterwards.
options.B: First check whether the client used the figure, then decide how urgent the correction is.
options.C: Correct it, assess the impact, alert the appropriate person, and coordinate the correction while protecting the other deadline.
options.D: Ask the client not to use the figure until you have finished the correction.

scenario: Two senior stakeholders each give you urgent work. You can complete only one to the required standard today, and neither knows about the other request.

options.A: Do the more senior person’s work first.
options.B: Start both and raise the conflict only if one clearly cannot be finished.
options.C: Clarify the deadlines and consequences, make the conflict visible early, and propose a realistic sequence.
options.D: Do the task with the nearest stated deadline and explain the delay to the other person afterwards.

scenario: A capable colleague keeps making the same small error. You have been fixing it, but the pattern is now affecting your own time.

options.A: Keep correcting it, but document the pattern in case it becomes serious.
options.B: Escalate it formally because the error has repeated.
options.C: Discuss it privately, understand what is causing it, agree a practical control, and review whether it stops.
options.D: Take over that part of the process while workload is busy.

scenario: A client wants softer wording in an accurate report. Their wording is technically true, but it would make a material risk much less obvious.

options.A: Use the client’s wording because the facts remain technically correct.
options.B: Keep the original wording exactly as it is.
options.C: Use neutral wording that keeps the material risk clear, and explain that boundary to the client.
options.D: Wait for a manager to decide which wording should be used.

scenario: An important task has a clear outcome but two unclear process steps. The person who assigned it will be unavailable for several hours.

options.A: Wait until the person is available.
options.B: Use the interpretation that seems most likely and correct it later if needed.
options.C: Complete the clear, reversible parts, document material assumptions, and seek clarification on what could affect the outcome.
options.D: Ask several colleagues and follow the majority view.

scenario: A core system fails 45 minutes before a time-sensitive submission. A manual workaround exists, but it creates reconciliation work later.

options.A: Keep retrying the system for as long as possible.
options.B: Notify affected people early, use the controlled workaround, and record what must be reconciled later.
options.C: Submit what is available on time, even if some fields are incomplete.
options.D: Log the issue with IT and wait because they own the system risk.

scenario: An employee asks for an exception because of a genuine personal difficulty. The rule allows some discretion, but inconsistent exceptions could create fairness concerns.

options.A: Apply the normal rule exactly so everyone is treated the same.
options.B: Grant the exception because the circumstances are genuine.
options.C: Use the allowed discretion consistently, document the reason, and apply the same principle to similar cases.
options.D: Refer the request upward because any exception is too risky.

scenario: Just before a leadership meeting, you notice an unusual value in a report. It may be genuine or an error, and there is not enough time for a full investigation.

options.A: Remove the value so it cannot distort the discussion.
options.B: Leave it in and add a note that it needs follow-up.
options.C: Do the quickest reasonable checks, then show it with the uncertainty and its possible effect clearly flagged.
options.D: Delay the entire report until the value can be fully verified.

scenario: A colleague admits a mistake that may affect a client financially and asks you to help fix it before telling a manager. The impact is not yet clear.

options.A: Help fix it first, then decide whether escalation is still necessary.
options.B: Report it immediately before doing anything else.
options.C: Quickly establish the likely impact, preserve the information, inform the appropriate person, and begin correction.
options.D: Tell the colleague it is their mistake and they must decide what to do.

scenario: A new process has slowed turnaround, but errors have also fallen. Some employees want to return to the old process after only two weeks.

options.A: Return to the old process until a better version is designed.
options.B: Keep the new process unchanged because resistance is normal.
options.C: Review speed, errors and user feedback together, then make targeted adjustments without losing the quality goal.
options.D: Keep it unchanged for another month before reacting.
